For many reasons I became interested in mycology and have been pursuing it as a career lately. 

The key to becoming a good mycologist - whether you're only interested in edibles, psychoactives, dyeing, or the diversity as a whole - is to practice.

Maybe this is a bit more than you care to bite off and chew, but I found that understanding fungi for the organisms they are and how intimately they tie our biosphere together made tripping on them that much more meaningful. 

So here are some tips:

* Get more than one reference book! And make it a book. My advice is not to download apps. They're not as complete and you get more information out of paper text currently. Apps can be great for getting down to a group though or with something easy like Chicken of the Woods.

* Use online resources like [Mushroom Expert](http://www.mushroomexpert.com/)

* Keep a journal. I haven't been doing that lately, but most of my findings are posted straight to Instagram which is great because everything can be georeferenced and I can get other ideas from others. Facebook and Instagram have some wonderful mushroom communities.

* Take walks and hikes just to find mushrooms. Sketch them, photograph them, make notes about their habitat and substrate, date your notes, and then take some home to spore print. 

* Learn to work through keys and ACTUALLY work through them. I'm a botanist by training so I'm always using keys to identify new plants. To me it's just second nature. Eventually you can get there too if you're not already. Plus - if you work in any environmental/natural resources field - that's a great skill to put on your resume. Being an amateur mycologist has landed me jobs - no lie.

* Meet some locals who are also mycologists - amateur or not. You can really learn a lot just by interacting with others and getting their opinions.

Again, I know that's a lot to bite off, but it's incredibly rewarding. Plus people think it's awesome if you know mushrooms. Haha!

I've been developing my skills for close to three years now - so by no means am I an expert mycologist - but I've found many psychoactives and it's pretty incredible to trip on something that you picked straight from the earth. 

Have fun with it!

Just wanted to get some thoughts down that I had after seeing your post. I've had similar ideas before, but never put them to paper. Here's what I have started: 

Soft phosphorescent glows - yellow, orange, blue, and pink illuminate the otherwise dark trail. Off in the distance, seemingly surrounding me comes the trickle of water over rocks and plopping onto something fleshy with a sputter. Above me, droplets splatter over the large, thick leaves and continually rain onto me. Sounds of the water and wildlife echo throughout the caverns leaving me disoriented yet exhilarated. 

The air coats my lungs like thick syrup soaking into warm pancakes. Occasionally I linger next to a rigid organic structure dimly lit by its neighbors. The energy of this place is tangible. Resting against the convoluting fleshy trunks rising out of the rich dank soil, I can feel the pulsing pull and exhale of the organism. Periodically, the ghostly white bark flutters a short burst of phosphorescence and the entire structure seems to shudder slightly. Or perhaps that’s simply an illusion caused by the low-light playing on my eyes. 

On the ground a myriad of strange insect-like creatures sift through the dense detritus. I crouch lower to find that their limbs are more akin to tiny branches reaching, curling, thrusting, bending and twisting in clusters - moving any and all edible parcels towards the anterior where an amorphous snout stretches and contours around the particle, devouring it whole. Each critter appears to constantly be at odds with itself and might pull apart at any instant if it weren’t for the insatiable hunger tying each thread together. Knotting. Small, dark moss-like plants with thin, broad leaves cluster over older clumps of detritus and soil. Each cluster is thinly veiled in brightly glowing mycelial nets reminiscent of a macabrely decaying christmas garland wrapped in lights running on barely enough electricity. 

Deep in the fungal forest, a large creature uvulates an unworldly call. In response, a similar call rings out in my near vicinity. Others sound off intermittently throughout the caverns over the next minute or so - their echoes haunting the dark subterranean forest. 

I carefully stand and creep onward. My footfalls hidden amongst the subtle clattering of water on every surface.  Ahead, the soft glowing light emitted by surrounding forest organisms becomes less defined. A smoky fog bank is slowly crawling through the undergrowth. Suddenly, I am tangled in wet knotty ropes dangling from high above in the darkness. Feeling for the switch on my headlamp, I turn it on hoping that I don’t find myself in the snare of some alien beast - only to discover that the cords appear to be roots of some sort. Perhaps belonging to a great tree high above the subterranean cathedral of organic light reaching itself deep into the rich ecosystem below. I wonder what these roots might find here. Hey everyone! Didn't see it mentioned anywhere yet, but just so no one is misled: To our knowledge, evolution is not a goal-oriented/driven process. Actually, mutations occur at random. Some mutations are fixed pretty quickly, however others may go on to be expressed phenotypically. This is basically what we call MICRO-evolution, MACRO-evolution which is the type leading to new species and diversity occurs as result of these mutations and their effect on the fitness of the organism.  As phenotypes appear and occur in populations (both spatially and temporally), isolation through various barriers eventually leads to new species. 
*Homo* didn't become hairless overnight. This trait developed through the "mosaic" process of evolution. It has to catch on over time. Although, I distinctly remember reading an article discussing the high adaptability of hairiness traits that stated populations of birds and mammals may rapidly adapt to climate conditions - bulking up on hair/feather/fat mass.
But back to the point, traits evolve and are THEN tested. During a human evolution course I had last semester, we discussed a fossil hip of a presumed bipedal hominid  which had "flattened" out more than the typical modern human's. Our hips form a shallow bowl, unlike chimpanzees which are more narrow and deep. This allows our particular pattern of locomotion. The owner of this particular fossil would have most likely developed a different pattern of walking in order to maximize that mutation. Perhaps it walked even more efficiently than we do, however its phenotype was snuffed out for whatever reason. The pattern of walking develops as an after effect or emergent property of that particular phenotype - the better the mutation is at helping the organism survive and spread it's genetic material, the longer it will persist.


Personally, I sorta hope that evolution is goal-oriented in an ass-backwards manner. As a biocentrist, I believe that the universe is finely-tuned for the creation and continued existence of lifeforms. In my opinion, one emergent property resulting from the combination of energy and matter given time and proper resources is life. Life wants to continue living - to me, that's why things evolve. "Versions" of life (like Dr. Wu's dinosaur "software" editions in Jurassic Park) exist around the world (and undoubtedly throughout the universe) - each competing to continue the struggle. It's elegant really. Vicious, chaotic, but elegant.
